extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and practitioners working on patent-domain tasks; patent professionals, patent examiners, and data scientists interested in automated patent text processing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation desiderata for automated patent-text tasks (summarization, translation, simplification, and generation), including dataset and modeling requirements specific to the legal/technical nature of patents. Emphasizes fidelity to legal language, readability, dataset/benchmark needs, and model design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarization: conciseness and informativeness tailored to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent summarization aims to create concise and informative summaries of patent documents that extract the most important information (e.g., claims, background, detailed descriptions) and paraphrase in more accessible language depending on the target audience (examiners, researchers, engineers, legal professionals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries should condense key aspects while remaining informative for the intended reader; choose level of technicality according to audience needs. Ensure essential legal/technical content (claims and their scope) is represented rather than only generic overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extractive summarization: preservation of original wording and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Extractive methods select key phrases or sentences verbatim from the patent text to retain the most significant and representative parts without altering wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: simpler implementation and preserves original terminology and precise legal phrasing. Cons/anti-patterns: can be disjointed and lack coherence; may fail when crucial information is implicit (not explicitly stated); can inherit the incomprehensibility of terse claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractive summarization: fluency and synthesis with factual fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstractive summarization rephrases documents into shorter texts that retain essential information, requiring deeper understanding and generation capability (e.g., sequence-to-sequence and transformer models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: can produce concise, fluent, and cohesive summaries by synthesizing information across the document. Risks/anti-patterns: higher chance of factual distortion, misinterpretation of domain-specific terms, misrepresenting legal nuances; computationally and data intensive. Use domain adaptation and careful factuality checks for patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM use in summarization: promising but patent-specific challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models have achieved strong summarization performance generally, but their performance on patent summarization is uncertain due to technical content and legal information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate LLM summaries for legal precision and domain terminology fidelity; do not assume general benchmarks guarantee adequate performance on patent-specific tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation: strict preservation of terminology and legal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent translation must convert patent texts between languages while preserving highly specialized technical jargon, precise terminology, and legal meaning so translated patents comply with different countries' legal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid synonym substitution or casual paraphrase that change feature-relevant language. Control generation variability (e.g., model temperature) to prevent unacceptable term variation. Prioritize terminological consistency and legal conformity over stylistic variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent translation dataset and parallel-corpus training
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective patent translation relies on training/evaluation datasets built from parallel patent documents and sentence alignments (e.g., EPO approaches, EuroPat corpus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patent-specific parallel corpora and mining strategies to generate training/eval data. Domain-specific corpora improve performance over general-domain machine translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing translation errors: pre- and post-processing for terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre- and post-processing methods can address common terminology and structural errors in machine-translated patent texts (e.g., identified types of terminology errors when translating English↔Chinese).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply source pre-editing to reduce terminology errors; incorporate terminology dictionaries or post-editing pipelines. Combine domain-specialized engines (Patent Translate) with general LLMs to leverage accuracy and coherence advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification: retain all information while improving readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent simplification aims to translate complex, technical, and legally precise patent language into simpler readable language while ideally retaining all original information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplified text should improve accessibility (remove jargon, rephrase technical terms) without losing essential details or legal scope. Watch for loss of subtle nuances or scope-broadening/narrowing changes as anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting-based simplification: claim trees and feature segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting methods improve accessibility by structuring claims into trees (dependencies), splitting claims into features, and visually representing which features are added by each claim; within-claim segmentation into preamble, transitional phrase, and body is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit claim references and linguistic analysis to build dependency graphs; segment claims into preamble/transitional/body to clarify structure. Visualizations (claim trees, feature highlighting) increase readability without modifying original texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraphrasing for simplification: controlled rewriting with minimal semantic drift
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrasing rewrites complex sentences into simpler versions (splitting, dropping, modifying) while keeping meaning unchanged, often via sequence-to-sequence models or rule-based patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply controlled paraphrase techniques (e.g., sentence splitting, controlled tokens for length/complexity). Anti-patterns: careless paraphrasing that loses terminological precision or legal nuances. Filter candidates and use domain-adapted models or post-filtering to avoid semantic drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent writing: legal precision, specificity, and section-aware generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated patent writing involves generating sections (title, abstract, claims, description) while meeting linguistic, technical, and legal complexities—language must be formal, unambiguous, precise, and adhere to office requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on titles or abstracts for claim generation (titles are too short; abstracts are often generic). Prefer description-based generation for claim drafting because descriptions contain detailed embodiments. Always plan for human revision to meet examination standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for generated patent text: completeness, clarity, logical linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of generated patent claims/text should be judged on completeness of claimed features, conceptual clarity, and logical linkage between description and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine-tuning models can improve completeness and clarity, but outputs typically require comprehensive human revision to pass legal scrutiny. Include checks for consistency with disclosed embodiments and formal claim structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and benchmarks: need for curated labeled datasets and standard metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent NLP requires extensive pre-structured, pre-processed high-quality labeled datasets and benchmarks (labeled datasets + established metrics) to enable reproducible and comparable evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices and researchers should provide open curated datasets for under-resourced tasks (e.g., novelty prediction, simplification). Benchmarks should include task-specific metrics beyond generic accuracy to reflect legal/technical requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for patent text generation: domain-specific metrics required
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing general-purpose text evaluation metrics may be inappropriate for patent texts because patents have specific legal and linguistic requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and adopt evaluation metrics that measure legal fidelity, terminological accuracy, claim completeness, and non-misleading paraphrase rather than relying solely on BLEU/ROUGE-type measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-sequence modeling: incorporate full patent descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent-analysis tasks focus on short parts (titles, abstracts) and ignore long descriptions, but descriptions contain detailed invention disclosure; models must handle long-range dependencies and very long contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate long-context LLMs or other long-sequence modeling approaches (models with extended context windows) to include patent descriptions. Evaluate trade-offs between context length, compute cost, and task benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal methods: integrate text, figures, and metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents include drawings, citations, and metadata; multimodal models can combine these modalities to improve tasks such as drafting, classification, and visualization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multimodal alignment (e.g., derive text from figures for drafting, link descriptions to diagrams) and exploit citations/metadata for richer features. Consider multimodal visualization tools to improve interpretability and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding choice: prefer sentence/paragraph embeddings for nuanced context
rubrics_metrics.description: For patent analysis, sentence/paragraph embeddings are preferred to word embeddings because they capture more nuanced contextual information from whole sentences or paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use higher-level embeddings for semantic tasks (classification, retrieval, novelty/creativity metrics) and avoid relying solely on word-level embeddings when context is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection and scaling: transformer-based models and computational trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformer-based models (BERT, GPT series) outperform many traditional ML models for patent text tasks; scaling to large LLMs improves performance but increases computational requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose model families based on task and resources: simpler tasks may use smaller transformers or classical models when compute is limited; for generation and deep semantic tasks, fine-tuned transformers or LLMs are preferred. Consider hybrid approaches and resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of novelty: align research metrics with legal novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Research notions of novelty (oddness, creativity, perceived originality) can differ from the strict legal definition used in patent law; some predictive metrics may not reflect statutory novelty or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing novelty/inventiveness predictors, explicitly align definitions and evaluation with patent-law standards; avoid treating surrogate metrics (semantic distance, unusualness) as direct measures of legal novelty without validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data access and preprocessing: need for high-quality structured patent data
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw patent publications (PDFs, poor scans, rudimentary classification) and restrictions on automated processing hinder training data quality; pre-processed, well-structured legal process documents and registries are necessary for better models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for patent-office provision of pre-processed corpora and improved access. In preprocessing pipelines, handle OCR errors, inconsistent metadata, and extract legal process documents (registers) to produce high-quality training/evaluation datasets.
